CRIME.
Six prisoners broke jail at Tyler, Tex., making the third escape within a month.

For an assault on a soap peddler following his show, Adam Forepaugh was fined $24.65 by a justice at Black River Falls, Wis.

For an article attacking the army, a journalist of Pesth has been sentenced to four months' imprisonment and fined one thousand florins.

Jackson Eastman, a prominent business man of Norfolk, Va., died from a stab from a pocket knife in the hands of Thomas Donald.

Otto Tooker, a Boston youth of 13, shot and killed a companion, Gustave Buettner, a boy of 16, with a toy pistol. The boys had a quarrel.

A report from Piedras Negras states that several American engineers have been killed in Mexico in consequence of disputes regarding right of way.

H. L. Smith, who lives in jail at Tupelo, Miss., under sentence to be hanged on July 18, has eaten nothing for twelve days, and declares he will starve to death.

In an affray between whites and blacks at Columbia, Va., a negro named Bill Hackney was struck on the head with a pick-handle and flung out of a window fifteen feet from the ground.

ManSFIELD, who was stabbed some three weeks ago by a Chinese laundryman in a dispute over the price for washing a shirt, is dying at the county hospital, Chicago.

The police of Cincinnati have jailed the proprietor of a turf exchange and five of his clerks for selling pools. Another operator and two clerks were arrested for putting up a board for the sale of combination pools.

—At Major J. B. Rawls' headquarters in Fort Brooke we saw an antiquated curiosity the other afternoon in the shape of a small swivel cannon which had been picked up recently on a reef near Tortugas in ten feet water. This gun is about three feet long, with a bore of about an inch and a half. It was pretty well incrusted with a coral growth of from one to three inches in thickness, showing that it had been a long, long time since it found a resting place in the Gulf. It may be a relic of the buccaneers or of some of the hardy adventurers of the long ago who sought the new world for conquest or plunder. The Major had also a preserved porcupine fish whose skin was studded with sharp spines of from one to two inches long. This curious fish is short, thick and broad, and this specimen when caught must have weighed 6 or 8 pounds. — Tampa Tribune.
Mr. D. S. Place, of Waldo, agent of the Bureau of Immigration, gave our citizens a little talk Wednesday night. We were promised the Secretary's report of the meeting, but he was suddenly called away on business. The report is good enough to keep and will appear next week. Our esteemed friend, Mr. John F. Dunn, was married at Lake Weir last Sunday to Miss Alice Eagleton, and the happe couple left on one of the Ocklawaha river boats for an extensive tour. They are now in New York, and will visit Saratoga, Niagara Falls, the White Mountains, etc., before their return. We hope the rarest blessings and sweetest pleasures will be theirs. The village of Leesburg was disturbed by a shooting affray one day this week, in which J. J. Dickinson, Jr., was shot three or four times with a pistol in the hands of a Mr. Blitch, and it is thought the wounds he received may prove fatal. The reports that reach us say that Mr. Dickinson was the aggressor; but before narrating the particulars as told us, we will wait the Advance's version of the affray. Ocala Banner.

If there are any idle carpenters in the world we would like a few of them to emigrate to Sumter county. The carpenters here now are insufficient to carry on the building to be done. We have two contractors in Leesburg, and both have work enough for the next twelve months without taking further orders, and that with a full set of hands each. With thribble the number of hands we now have there would be thribble the amount of building. Our exchanges will do us a favor by copying this item and giving it a good circulation.—The first subscriber in Sumter county to the Confederate monument at Tallahassae was a soldier who wore the blue.—There is no doubt but that the Peninsular Railway will soon be completed to Lake Panasoffkee. It will pass through one of the most productive sections of our county, where corn, cotton, oranges and vegetables grow prolifically. We congratulate our citizens that the iron horse will soon place them in quick transit with the great cities of the Union where their products can be profitably marketed.—Leesburg Advance. —The car shops of the Florida Southern Railway, in this place, for the First Division have been finished. Dimensions of buildings 80x36 feet. The machine shop is also up, and the construction of the round-house and turn-table will be commenced immediately. Seven box and twenty flat cars are now being built in these shops, which will have a carrying capacity of 30,000 pounds, nearly as much again as that of the broad gauge. The order for fifty additional cars is now out, and iron for the same is being turned out by the Tredigar Works at Richmond, Va., and will arrive here about the latter part of July or the first of August. A number of passenger, express and box cars will reach here at the same time. The iron on this road has been laid a distance of twenty-eight miles, and the trains are running daily. The following are the stations along the line, with distances from Palatka to Gainesville, viz: To Francis, 5 miles; to MacWilliams, 12 miles; to Blue Pond, 17 miles; to Johnson, 23 miles; to McMeekin, 26 miles; to Waites' Crossing, 30 miles; to Magnesia Springs, 35 miles; to Perry, 38 miles; to Tarver, 45 miles; to Gainesville, 50 miles. — Palatka Herald.

dickerson-leesburg.A2:
A Florida Lynching.
JACKSONVILLE, FLA., July 16.—Some weeks ago J. J. Dickinson, Jr., son of General Dickinson, late Adjutant-General of Florida, had a difficulty with a saloon-keeper named Beach in Leesburg, Sumter county. It was apparently adjusted at the time, but was renewed by Dickinson last Tuesday, when he took advantage of Beach and fired two shots from a double-barrelled gun at him and made his escape, supposing he had killed him. Beach was severely but not dangerously wounded. Dickinson was captured and lodged in Leesburg jail. At 2 o'clock yesterday morning an armed and disguised mob of twenty-five men appeared at the jail, overpowered the jailer, and shot Dickinson twice in prison. They then took him outside and riddled him with bullets.

The Lynching of Young Dickison.
In our telegraphic columns appears a dispatch from Jacksonville, Fla., announcing the death of J. J. Dickison, Jr., son of Gen. Dickison, late Adjutant General of Florida, at the hands of a mob, who took him from the jail at Leesburg, where he had been confined on the charge of having shot a saloon-keeper named Beach. This young man will doubtless be remembered by many of our citizens. His father, General Dickison, shortly after the war, removed from Florida to Savannah, and for a number of years carried on the factorage and commission business on the Bay. Young Dickison was a clerk with his father, and his career here made him generally known. Gen. Dickison returned to Florida, and was appointed Adjutant General under Governor Drew, and is a gentleman not only highly thought of here, but in Florida.
dickerson-leesburg.A12:
John Dickison Killed.
We learn from a detailed account of the affair in the Union of Sunday, that J. J. Dickison, Jr., the son of General J. J. Dickison, of Quincy, who had become engaged in a personal difficulty with a man named Beach at Leasburg, at whom he had fired, was taken from the jail, under the erroneous impression that Beach was fatally wounded, and lynched, by a party of armed and disguised men.

This unfortunate and horrible affair is the first instance known in the State where there was so little shadow of excuse for arbitrary or violent measures; and brings upon the aged surviving parents of the victim a sorrow that will follow them through life, and in which they have the sincerest sympathy and confluence of a large circle of devoted friends in this section where they have resided so long.

Words fail to adequately express the horror and condemnation felt by all good citizens for the commission of such a crime against law, good order and civilization.

For the past three weeks our town has been under excitement over the first attempt of Mr. J. J. Dickison, Jr., to kill Mr. Lewis Beach.

We will here give a short sketch of his career in Leesburg previous to this time. More than a year ago he came to Leesburg, having to secretly leave Quincy for shooting a negro. As he became acquainted with the people, it was found he had a generous disposition, but with it he was tyrannical and overbearing, especially when drinking. He had not been here long before it was evident to everyone's mind that he was a desperate man, and was pronounced by the community to be a desperado and outlaw, as he had defied the law on every occasion. His career was such that people feared him; they were uneasy whenever he came to town, for as soon as he began to drink he began to fuss with any and everybody, and no one knew at what time he would attempt to kill them. About the middle of June he attempted to draw the town Marshal into a difficulty. He drew his pistol and asked him to do the same, cursing him, calling him a coward and defying him to attempt to arrest him. The Marshal told him not to shoot; that he had nothing against him, and did not want to arrest him. We were present on this occasion, and Colonel Smith also. We both did all in our power to get him off, but did not succeed until he had insulted the Marshal in every way possible.

The particulars in the affair with Mr. Beach are as follows: On the 28th of June Mr. Dickison came to the barroom of Mr. S. W. Wallace, where Mr. Beach was staying, and threw an empty beer keg through the door and blinds, making a fearful racket. Mr. Beach came out and accused him of the act. Dickison denied it, and at the same time drew his pistol and asked Beach if he wished to shoot it out. Beach saw the weapon in his face and drew his also. Dickison seeing that Beach had an equal showing with him, proposed to replace the pistols and let the matter drop. Beach was only too glad to comply, and, believing Dickison to be a man of honor, and relying on what he said, accepted the treaty of peace; but Dickison only sought to gain the advantage, for no sooner did Beach put up his pistol than Dickison drew his and fired, fortunately without effect. Beach returned the fire, striking Dickison in the arm. Dickison stepped aside, out of range of Beach's pistol, and fired, but again without effect. Dickison then ran, and Beach followed him, firing two other shots, but missed, when Dickison disappeared in the dark. Dickison was arrested the day after, and set at liberty under simply a peace bond of $500. His wound was cared for by Dr. Stevens, and when he left town he said that the affair was not through with, although he had sent for Beach, made friends and expressed much sorrow at what had occurred. This statement is certified to by several witnesses. Dickison came to town several times after and acted in a way to lead every one to believe that he intended to attempt Beach's life. The suspicions of the people were so thoroughly aroused that they went to Beach and warned him not to have any intercourse with Dickison. Beach listened to this counsel only partially, for on Monday night, July 11th, Dickison called Beach out back of Baer's store to converse with him. The discourse was strictly of a friendly nature, which threw Beach entirely off his guard. Dickison stepped off from Beach about thirty feet and began to feel around as if looking for something. Beach asked him what he was doing, when he said: "Beach, God d—n you, you have said enough to me," and raised a shot gun, which he had concealed, and fired. Beach received the load in the shoulder, and Dickison, thinking he had killed him, ran off. Beach gave the alarm, and the Mayor sent a posse of men in hot pursuit, for it was the most cold blooded attempt to murder ever perpetrated in this county. Beach's shoulder was filled with buckshot, and two of his arm bones were broken. He is now under the treatment of Dr. Stevens, and is doing as well as could be expected.

Dickison had made threats to take the lives of no less than six of our good citizens, for no reason whatever. The names of these parties we could mention if necessary. One of the parties in particular he said he intended to kill while asleep in bed. The day he shot Beach, while coming to town he shot at a negro just to try the gun
One of the parties in particular he said he intended to kill while asleep in bed. The day he shot Beach, while coming to town he shot at a negro just to try the gun he shot Beach with. He hailed the negro and told him he wished to try his gun. The negro jumped behind a tree, which saved his life. The load from his gun was buried in the tree behind which the negro stood.

With the attempt to murder Beach and knowing the threats he had made, the citizens determined to capture him if possible. The Sheriff summoned a posse and began the pursuit Tuesday morning. The woods around his house were scoured and he was routed Tuesday noon, but the party did not get up with him. They learned that he had crossed the Ocklawah river, secured a mule and was heading for Ocala, and the chase was hotly pursued on horseback, about twelve in the party. They finally struck his trail, and after riding hard all Wednesday night found him at daylight Thursday morning. Dickison was asleep in a house, which was surrounded, when he was summoned to surrender. He had a shot-gun with him, and for a short while he thought of making a rush on the party, kill as many as he could and make his escape. Knowing this would be certain death to himself, he finally surrendered. He was brought to Leesburg Thursday evening and lodged in jail with a strong guard placed over him, and now we are palmed to chronicle his doom. About two o'clock Friday morning a masked body of men, numbering between twenty-five and thirty, overpowered the guards, forced them to open the door, and shot Dickison with double-barrel guns.

We do not approve of lynch law, and are sorry that this community had to resort to such extreme measures. We have sketched the foregoing short account of Dickison's career in Leesburg to let the world know why such severe measures were resorted to, and as the deed is done a number of our most influential citizens have requested us to give an impartial statement of Mr. Dickison's career, showing that this county is not lawless, but law-abiding, and that they feel much relieved at the death of Mr. Dickison, for no man's life with whom he came in contact was safe.

After the Coroner's inquest, which rendered a verdict that he came to his death by shots from guns in the hands of unknown parties, his remains were interred in Lone Oak Cemetery.

The Promotionists experienced signal defeat in the North Carolina election.

Government Churchill of Arkansas, has declared martial law in Perry county, the scene of the recent disturbances.

The "blind mosquitoes" are so plentiful in Palatka, that the Herald was delayed in the appearance of its last issue.

Two Steamboats, the Idlewild, valued at $25,000, and the Osceola Belle, valued at $20,000 were burned at Memphis on the 31st inst.

A bill has been introduced in the Georgia Legislature chartering a railroad from Rome in that State, to St. Marks, Florida, via. Tallahassee.

The St. Augustine Press office was struck by lightning a few days ago, tearing off a plank, and giving one of the editor's fingers an electric shock.

Mayor King, of Philadelphia, appointed four colored men to the police force on the 5th, the first of their race to to wear police uniform in that city.

The DeLand Agriculturist says that a large number of colored people are employed on the orange groves about there, and so far they have behaved remarkably well.

Major-General Hancock has been appointed by Secretary-of-War Lincoln to take charge of the military display at Yorktown Centennial Celebration in October.
Frank V. Evans, Esq., formerly of the Albany (Ga.) Advertiser, has removed his family to Birmingham, where he will start a new paper. He is a clever gentleman and a good newspaper man.

The lynching of the son of our ex-Adjutant-General, John Dickerson, says the Manatee News, is an event to be deplored and should at once be handled without gloves by our executives of the law.

John Russell Young tells Gath that Gen. Grant's income is about $50,000 a year from his son's firm, in which Grant is a silent partner, from his railroad positions, his own investments and the Grant fund.

The large cotton-shed of A. P. Wright & Co., at Thomasville, which was consumed by fire, together with 1400 bales of cotton, a few days ago, is now being rebuilt. It will be 150 feet wide by 197 long.

Leo Hartman, the notorious Russian Nihilist, who reached this country a fugitive from justice a few days since, has since fled to Canada, fearing arrest. As there is no treaty of extradition between this country and Russia, he need not have been so hasty.

Second Assistant Postmaster-General Elmer reports a net reduction in the Star route and steamboat mail service during the month of July amounting to $314,664, and that the total amount of savings by the reductions and discontinuances since March 4th is $1,381,442.

Apopka Citizen: "A public meeting should be held in every town in Florida in the interest of government, to condemn, most roundly, the Leesburg tragedy, and every outlawry act committed in the State. Let the public sentiment of Florida be thus made known."

Is the rumor true that Bisbee has determined to back out of his contest with Finley since the Supreme Court has decided that the votes of all of the convicted thieves in his district could not have saved him? Is there no one to speak for Bisbee? No, not one.

The war of rates between the great rival railway lines continues without any signs of abatement or compromise. A person can travel first-class now from Boston to Chicago for five dollars. The competing routes keep a close watch upon each other, and a reduction of rates by one is quickly followed by a lower cut on the part of its rivals.

The Georgia people are considerably exercised about the operations of the Mormons in that State. They will not be able to accomplish anything legally, as the constitution and laws forbid interference with any citizen's religious belief, and the Mormons claim that Mormonism is a religion. The only remedy is to get together and hustle them out of the State, nolens volens. That's the way the Illinois anti-mormons did in 1846.

—The Sunland Tribune says: "A lawyer who has investigated the subject informs us that he thinks there can be no question of the constitutional right of the Legislature to tax the improvements on the U. S. lands as personal property, for the reason that he owns the improvements as separate and distinct from the land, and, therefore, has it in his power to dispose of them as he pleases without it being a trespass on the land."

Speaker A. O. Bacon is of the opinion that the Legislature can get through with its work in forty days, if not sooner.

Hon. Welborn Price, of Oconee, favors early and late sessions of the General Assembly, and a rest during the hot part of the day. He suggests a morning session from 8 to 12 o'clock, and an evening session from 4:30 to 7 o'clock. This would give ample working hours in the coolest part of the day, and expedite the transaction of business.

Col. William M. Wadley, President of the Central Railroad, reached Columbus on Wednesday morning in a special car, and left at 5 o'clock in the afternoon for Troy. Ala.

Col. J. E Jones, at the Central Georgia Bank, Macon, is engaged in issuing the $32.50 scrip dividends due upon the Southwestern Railroad stock.

Fine rains visited Burke county last week, and the farming outlook has materially brightened thereby. Farmers wear a more cheerful look.

The crops, of all kinds, in Cobb county are better than they have been in thirty years.

A horrible tale of ravishment and mutilation is related by the Chattanooga Times as having occurred on Missionary Ridge a few days ago, perpetrated upon the person of Miss Nancy Donaldson, 17 years of age, by a mulatto demon named Henry Lawson, who had a wife and five children. The young lady was also horribly mutilated with a razor, which the villain used to cut, disfigure and terrify her whenever she screamed. He was pursued, captured and imprisoned to await trial.

It is announced that Rev. S. P. Callaway, editor and proprietor of the State Line Press, at West Point, has bought the LaGrange Reporter.

The Walton Vidette says: "Among the numerous questions for consideration by the Legislature is a bill which will probably be presented, to make from the Blue Ridge and the Western Circuits a new Judicial Circuit. This is the largest circuit in the State, having eleven counties and a population of 124,000 souls. Few men are physically able to hear and decide the business of so many people in fifty-two weeks."

With the convict question, the Railroad Commissioners, the Lunatic Asylum, the temperance question, the fence question, the State capitol, the new circuit and a host of local measures, the Legislature is likely to need all the time allowed for the session.

There has been a great deal of sickness in Campbell county for the past week or two. The health of that community is improving, however, as most of those who were complaining have recovered.

Newnan Herald: "There were thirteen colored persons arrested on the excursion train on the 4th for carrying firearms. Five of these were turned over to Sheriff Anderson and lodged by him in Coweta jail."

Watkinsville Advance: "Mr. Sam Harris, Acting Deputy Sheriff, arrested Joe Walker last Monday and lodged him in jail, under a warrant sworn out by G. C. Thomas, Esq., charging him with killing a cow."

Eastman Times: "We learn from a reliable source that the boiler of the steam saw mill on the Dodge road in Telfair county exploiled last Friday, killing one colored man instantly. The cause was a defect in the boiler, and is not attributable to negligence."

Jenkinsville correspondence of the Barnesville Gazette: "We have had good rains, and corn and cotton are booming. As sweet potato seed nearly all rotted last winter, the potato crop will be a failure with us. Wheat is turning out very sorry."

Barnesville Gazette: "The prosperity of the colored people of Barnesville is indicated by the progress they are making in the purchase of lots and building residences thereon. Several colored persons are now building houses for themselves and families."

Newnan Herald: "Neither of the darkkeys who broke jail last week has been captured. Their names and crimes are as follows: Sam Foster, hog stealing; Henry Jones, violating United States revenue laws; Henry Casper, enticing contract hands; Wade Brooks, larceny."

Covington Enterprise: "Nathan Whitley is perhaps the oldest man in this part of the State. His birth is put down in the old family Bible, and by that record he is one hundred and one hundred. He is as heales a man of sixty
perhaps the oldest man in this part of the State. His birth is put down in the old family Bible, and by that record he is one hundred and two years old. He is as hale as a man of sixty and appears to take the world easy. He says the times are no harder now than they were when he was a boy."

North Georgia Citizen: "All along the route from Dalton to Beaverdale the crops are growing splendidly. We never saw corn and cotton looking so well, and what wheat has and is being harvested is very fine. Here, as everywhere else, there is an abundance of cotton—too much, we think, for the welfare of that section."

North Georgia Citizen: "We passed through Catoosa county last week, and were gratified to find that the farmers have not, like the farmers of their neighboring counties, gone wild on the cotton planting question. We saw only a few patches of the fleecy staple, but plenty of corn, all of which promises an abundant yield."

Franklin News: "The gentleman who brought the mail from Carrollton on the 4th reported that a Mr. McMullen was mortally stabbed at that place on Saturday evening by a Mr. Hanvey, and died on Sunday evening. Dr. Gaulding, of Carrollton, who was in Franklin yesterday, confirms the report. The men had been drinking."

Griffin News: "We learn there was a lively row, on the 1st inst., at Camp Stephens, in which about a dozen negroes were engaged. A man and his wife 'fell out,' words ensued, and a fight resulted. The neighbors rushed in and made the business rather promiscuous. Some of the parties have been arrested, and will have a hearing before the court."

Atlanta Post-Appeal: "The men who think that good milk can be given by cows that prowl about the central portion of the city eating trash out of barrels and boxes and drinking water from sewers and cess pools in the streets, should cast their eyes upon the two miserable looking specimens now rambling about the Union passenger depot."

Campbell County News Letter: "Mr. Walt Smith, of Union District, in this county, had the misfortune to lose two fine mules last Tuesday week by getting them choked to death. He had tied them together by the neck with a rope and turned them out to graze, and by some means they became entangled in the rope and were thrown to the ground, and when he found them one was dead and the other so nearly so that it died in about an hour."

Columbus Times: "A few nights ago a difficulty occurred in this city between Calvin Saxon and two brothers, Charles and Joe Prather, in which they were all more or less used up. Saxon received a cut in the face, and hatchet to good effect upon his go
gently occurred in this city between Calvin Saxon and two brothers, Charles and Joe Prather, in which they were all more or less used up. Saxon received a cut in the face, and he used a hatchet to good effect upon his assailants. He sued out a warrant for the arrest of the Prathers, but one of them has left the city, and we understand that the other one has since been confined to his room by his wound.'

Cuthbert Enterprise: "Very material improvements and additions are now being made to the Agricultural College. All the front part has already been nicely and ta-tefully repainted. The rear end of the chapel has been taken out and an extension made beyond its former limits of about twenty feet. The new tower is now near completion and ready for the painter. The entire building, up stairs and below, has been nicely plastered, and the grails present a beautiful appearance."

TELEGRAPHIC NEWS.
CHATTANOOGA TENN., July 11.—A well known physician of this city, Dr. Jas. E. Baily, shot and probably mortally wounded Charles Marsh, a carpenter. They are neighbors and their wives quarreled about some trivial matter. This the husbands took up, which resulted in their mortal combat to-day.

A negro name Hugh Lawson, who raped a young lady last week and mutilated her body in a most fiendish manner, has been arrested and lodged in jail. There is great danger of his being lynched. A mob of men congregated in front of the jail last night with that purpose in view, but were deterred by a strong sheriff's guard. Excitement is still high, however.

LITTLE ROCK, ARK., July 11.—Sunday morning Frank Conway, lessee of the Johnson plantation, twelve miles from this place, was shot and dangerously wounded by one of his workmen, named Walters, with whom he was quarrelling. Conway is widely known, being a nephew of ex Gov. Conway; of this city.

CINCINNATI, July 11—The United States signal service themometer here registered 103.5 at 3:15 yesterday afternoon. Ordinary thermometers registered from 7 to 8 degrees higher in the shade. The heat was the greatest on record here. This coroner was called to attend thirteen deaths, all from congestion of the brain, supposed to have been superinduced by the excessive heat. There were twelve sunstrokes, though no fatal cases were reported up to midnight. In Covington, Ky., there were six cases of sunstroke yesterday, four of them fatal.

CANTON, Miss., July 11.—From reliable information received and dispatches seen Neshoba county, on Saturday, instructed for Major Barksdale for Governor. Forty-five delegates, out of fifty-two, in Lowndes county are for Stone for Governor, and in Lincoln county forty out of fifty country delegates are for J. M. Stone for Governor, Gwin for auditor, and Myers for secretary of state.

HOUSTON, TEXAS, July 11.—Justice Brashear has been engaged all day in the examination of the case of Bob White, colored, and W. H. Cowhart, suspected of having murdered W. H. Gleason, about two days ago. Gleason was found floating in the Bayou with his head cut off, his bowels removed and otherwise mutilated. The body was naked and had a piece cut from the breast, another from the arm and another from the leg. It was reported to-day that Gleason had his name tattooed on his body with India ink just where these cuts were made, and that the white man Cowhart knew of them. There was other strong circumstancial evidence pointing to Cowhart as the murderer.

FREDERICKSBURG, VA., July 11.—Silas Massey (colored) was shot in the breast and instantly killed on Saturday, near Acqua creek, Stafford county, by Capt. S. S. Lee. Massey was unmercifully beating a white woman, his paramour, with a heavy stick, threatening to kill her, when Capt. Lee commanded him to desist. The negro then assailed Capt. Lee with great violence, and in trying to protect himself the fatal wound was inflicted by Capt. Lee. An inquest was held by a jury, composed of white and colored men, which rendered a verdict that the killing was done in self-defense.

Death Sentence for Rape
Death Sentence for Rape
Henry Lawson, the black fiend accused of rape upon the person of Miss Nancy Donaldson, in Hamilton County, July 4, was convicted of the crime in the circuit court at Chattanooga, Tuesday last, the jury returning a verdict of guilty, without extenuating circumstances, fixing the punishment at hanging, from which an appeal will be taken.
The judge was to pass the sentence yesterday, and fix the date.
hugh-lawson-chattanooga-1881-07-10.A8: Henry Lawson, the regro rapist and murderer, who was sentenced to be hanged last week, will be hung in Chattanooga on Friday, Sept. 2nd.
